leaves.name: Marble Canyon Ice
leaves.blurb: Marble Canyon Ice is a winter venue in the Cariboo region of south-central British Columbia, in a limestone canyon on the Lillooet and Cache Creek side of Highway 99. It is a long day trip from Vancouver. The 14 climbs are mostly mixed lines, with M grades running from the mid-range up to M9, plus a few ice routes that range from WI2 to WI6. Several lines can be top-roped, which is unusual for ice on the west coast, so the main wall can draw a crowd on winter weekends. A short walk gets you to the base, and the top of the ice is visible from the lake edge.

leaves.name: Diamond Lake (ICE)
leaves.blurb: Diamond Lake is the centrepiece of winter climbing in the Bancroft and Madawaska region of eastern Ontario. The ice faces rise above a flat lake, and the walk in is across the frozen surface, so check the thickness first. Seventeen routes are listed, nearly all water ice and most of them around WI4, with a few easier lines at WI1 to WI3 and a small number of mixed routes ranging from easy to very hard. The setting is scenic, and the variety of lines is what keeps climbers returning. Sunny days can warm the crag noticeably, and how many lines form depends heavily on the winter.

leaves.name: Tahquitz Ice & Surrounding Flows
leaves.blurb: These are the winter water-ice and mixed flows on and around Tahquitz Rock and Suicide Rock above Idyllwild in Southern California. Most of the 14 listed routes are around WI3, with a few easier lines, and one much harder flow up near the top of the scale. Some run to several hundred feet or more, and unless the ice is very fat, many climb as mixed routes. The ice is unreliable: it takes heavy snowfall followed by cold nights and freeze-thaw cycles, and it does not form every winter. Parties start very early, since daytime warmth thaws the flows. The Trough is the most consistent of them, at about 500 feet.

leaves.name: Big Thompson Canyon Ice
leaves.blurb: These winter flows hang beside US 34 between Loveland and Estes Park, at roughly 6,700 feet. The ice sits fairly high on a south-facing hillside and the walk in is short and easy, although getting across the river is the hard part until it freezes solid. Of the 19 lines, most are WI2 or WI3, with one WI4, a couple of WI5s and a single M4 mixed line. That moderate spread makes it a friendly place to learn ice or take first leads. Two distinct pitches form reliably; it is mainly a local-weekend venue.

leaves.name: Cathedral Ledge Ice Climbs
leaves.blurb: Cathedral Ledge towers above North Conway and is one of the White Mountains' best-known winter venues. This part of the cliff offers about a dozen ice lines, with a smattering of mixed climbing, in a spread from WI2 up to WI5. Most of the routes fall at WI4, so it suits climbers who have moved past the beginner flows, while a couple of easier lines and a few harder pillars give variety on either side. Ice here forms in winter only, and the road up the cliff is shut, so plan on walking in.

leaves.name: Kinsman Notch Ice (aka Luck O' The Irish crag)
leaves.blurb: A winter ice and mixed crag in Kinsman Notch, above Route 112 near North Woodstock. Fifteen climbs are packed fairly close together: nine ice routes, mostly WI3 to WI4 with one at WI5, and six mixed lines from M5 up to M9. Thick woods keep sun off the ice and shelter the crag from wind. A steep path climbs from the road to the base, where crampons help when it is icy. The crag splits into a right-hand section near the top of the trail and a second section farther left. Many routes are easy to top-rope from trees, and weekends can get busy.
leaves.name_search: kinsman notch ice aka luck o the irish crag
leaves.parking_note: Pull off beside Route 112 in the notch; a steep climbers' path leads up to the crag from there.

leaves.name: Humphrey's Ledge Ice Climbs
leaves.blurb: A small winter cliff a short drive beyond Cathedral Ledge in the North Conway valley, useful when the bigger walls are crowded. Nearly all of its 18 climbs are water ice, running from easy WI2 up to WI4, with most sitting at WI3 and a handful at WI4. One mixed line at the easy end rounds out the list. It sits low in the valley, with a modest elevation of a few hundred feet above sea level, so it suits climbers looking for moderate ice in a quieter setting than the main ledges.

leaves.name: Whiteside (ice)
leaves.blurb: These are the winter ice lines on Whiteside Mountain, a big granite dome between Cashiers and Highlands in the southern Blue Ridge. The ice forms on the shaded north side and in gullies, and conditions vary a lot from season to season, so check the local weather before driving out. Twenty ice routes run from WI2 up to WI5, but most sit in the WI3 to WI4 range, with only two at the top end. The best-known line is a long, often thin two-pitch climb. On a cold day you can ice climb in the shade while the sunny south side is warm enough for rock.

leaves.name: Joe's Valley Ice Climbs
leaves.blurb: Winter ice around Joe's Valley Reservoir in central Utah, with most of the flows in Straight Canyon or right beside the reservoir. About eleven climbs, almost all water ice plus a single hard mixed line. The ice runs from WI3 through WI5, with the WI4s the most common, so there is something for climbers stepping up as well as those after a steeper pillar. The ice forms against a sandstone backdrop, and conditions can change quickly, so reading the ice and avoiding wet rock matters. Expect post-holing on some approaches when snow is deep, and busy weekends at the best-known flows.

leaves.name: The Box Canyon Ice Climbs
leaves.blurb: A side canyon off Maple Canyon in central Utah that fills with winter ice. All 18 climbs here are water ice, running from easy WI2 and WI3 steps up through a solid middle block of WI4 and WI5 to a few WI6 lines, so it suits climbers with some experience more than first-timers. Walls rise several hundred feet, and the harder routes are bigger and more serious than the ones along the main canyon road. Whether anything is in condition depends on snowfall and a melt and refreeze cycle, and it can change fast. Plan on two ropes for the rappels.
leaves.name_search: the box canyon cyn ice climbs
leaves.approach: Walk up the canyon road from the entrance, a little under a mile, to the side canyon on the right. The road is often snow covered in ice season, so expect to hike or ski.

leaves.name: Providence Canyon Ice
leaves.parking_note: Winter ice access: the canyon road is unpaved and only the bottom half mile is plowed. Park at the lot half a mile up, which fills with snowmobile trailers on weekends; the climbs are near an old limestone quarry about 2.25 miles beyond.

leaves.name: Santaquin Canyon Ice
leaves.blurb: Santaquin Canyon Ice is a winter venue in the southern Wasatch, with twelve ice lines and six mixed climbs. Most flows sit on the shaded south side of the canyon, and a lot of them can be seen from the road. Ice grades centre on WI4, with a few easier and several harder lines up to the WI6 range, while the mixed routes cover a wide band from moderate M-grades into double digits. Many climbs are one or two pitches, and the lines tend to run in gullies that can slide, so avalanche conditions matter a great deal. Snowmobile traffic and weekend crowds are common.

leaves.name: Banks Lake Ice Climbing
leaves.blurb: Roadside waterfall ice along State Route 155 between Coulee City and Grand Coulee, on the basalt walls of the coulee in central Washington. Most flows are visible from the car and need only a short walk. Grades run from WI3 up to WI6, with the largest group at WI5 and a fair number of WI4 lines. Flows come in only after a sustained cold snap, so the season is brief and some winters give very little. Ice quality ranges from plastic to brittle, many climbs finish in brush, and the biggest flows shed ice as the day warms, so early starts are wise.

leaves.name: Winter-Spring (ice, snow
leaves.blurb: Chair Peak (6,238 ft) is a rugged, castellated summit in the Snoqualmie Pass area of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cascade Range, about 3 miles northwest of Snoqualmie Pass and immediately south of Snow Lake. Its steep faces are granodiorite of the Snoqualmie Batholith (intruded ~28-22 million years ago), sculpted by Pleistocene glaciation into short, exposed alpine lines popular for their proximity to Seattle. The peak was first climbed in 1913 by Hec V. Abel and L.F. Curtis; this area groups the peak's winter-spring ice, snow and mixed routes rather than a separate summit.
